opening.headline: Understanding why a single defense mechanism is insufficient, and determining whether combining input validation, context isolation, output validation, and permission restrictions provides sufficient protection.
body: There is an agent with only one input filter. If an expression falls outside the filter's recognition, it passes through unchanged. There are also instructions that enter via paths not going through the filter, such as the body of a web page. After passing through, there is no mechanism to block tool calls.

This lesson distinguishes between the concepts of defense layers and the specific failures each of the four layers is responsible for. Next, we learn to read the guardrails and approval settings in the OpenAI Agents SDK, and we develop three questions to assess whether a defense composition is sufficient. Finally, we examine the flow of defense by explaining how the next layer blocks an attack even if a hole exists in one layer.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Input validation, context isolation, output validation, and permission restrictions can be categorized as defense layers.
It is possible to determine whether a defense composed of multiple layers is sufficient.

screens.title: A single defense is insufficient.
screens.lead: First, take a look at the situation of an agent with just one input filter. The diagram shows both the paths that go through the filter and those that do not go through it.

visual.alt: User input is filtered, but the web content bypasses the filter and reaches the model and refund tools.

paragraphs: The customer support agent is protected by a single filter. The filter filters out known circumvention expressions, and the team can rest assured. However, this agent is capable of web searching and also has a refund tool.

If a new expression unknown to the filter is received, it will pass through unchanged. The main body of the web page appears as part of the tool results later, so it does not go through the filter at the initial input stage. After passing both of these stages, there is no mechanism to block a refund tool call.
The question for this class is this: How do we combine multiple defenses, and how do we determine if they are sufficient?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When one defense is breached, it's important to understand how much damage extends. Defenses are evaluated not by their blocking power, but by the extent of damage after being penetrated.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how many layers our defense currently has.

screens.title: What is the current defense thickness?
screens.lead: When a question is selected, the instructor's thoughts are presented. There are no input or submission fields, so first reflect on your own system.

items.prompt: What is our current defense level?
items.answer: Upon closer inspection, it turns out to be less than expected. Often, it consists merely of prompt rules and input filters. Rather than counting the number of layers, the starting point is to document what specific role each layer assumes.

items.prompt: Does each overlap block a different point, or does it block the same point twice?
items.answer: Placing two input filters is equivalent to blocking the same point twice. If an input filter misses a path, both filters will miss that path. Defense in depth is designed to overlap at different points—specifically, at input, context, output, and permissions.

items.prompt: If one layer is breached, is there a subsequent barrier mechanism?
items.answer: The last question is whether there are approvals or scope restrictions before tool calls. Even if all previous layers are penetrated, if there exists a filter that blocks the call before execution, the damage mitigation will be reduced. If no such filter exists, having numerous layers is insufficient.

screens.outro: Now, let's verify the four layers of defensive depth with a diagram.

screens.title: Defense layers and four tiers
screens.lead: When you select the diagram number marker, a description will open explaining at which point and what the corresponding layer blocks. Please review all five layers and the overall principle.

visual.alt: A diagram showing four layered stages numbered sequentially: input validation, context isolation, output validation, and permission restriction, flowing from input to output.
labels: The damage limit is defined by authorization, even if all layers are compromised.

markers.label: Input check
markers.title: Layer 1: Input validation
markers.body: Input guardrails, safety screens, and known-pattern filters fall into this category. By quickly filtering out inputs using a lightweight model before invoking more expensive models, cost savings can be achieved. However, note that input guardrails apply only to the initial input received by the first agent in the chain.

markers.label: Context separation
markers.title: Layer 2: Context Isolation
markers.body: Packages the untrusted content into tool_result, discloses the source, and wraps it in JSON. Including explanations such as inbound email or unknown sender in the JSON's source field enables the model to understand the nature of the text, and JSON escaping clearly demarcates the boundary between the body and structure. Our instruction places the content inside tool_result, not in the following user turn.

markers.label: Output check
markers.title: Layer 3: Output Inspection
markers.body: Output guardrails are executed after final output is completed. Sensitive information is masked, and if a streaming classifier intervenes, stop_reason becomes refusal, so the context is reset and processing continues. However, there is a limitation that previously executed tool calls cannot be blocked.

markers.label: Permission restrictions
markers.title: Layer 4: Permission Restrictions and Approvals
markers.body: Minimum privilege, sandboxing, and approval for tools with side effects fall into this category. Even if a call is made, it will not execute if it exceeds its scope, and calls requiring approval are halted. This is the final layer that defines the damage limit when all previous layers have been compromised.

markers.label: principles
markers.title: Each layer is responsible for different failures.
markers.body: Defense stacking refers to a design where multiple defenses are layered at different points to ensure that if one defense fails, the next one can still prevent the attack. Input validation checks for failures of known inputs, context separation prevents confusion between instructions and data, output validation detects failures in the model-generated sentences, and permission restrictions bear the responsibility for potential damage caused by actions. Simply overlapping defenses at the same point does not constitute defense stacking.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the location of the layer, I'll now review how it is set in the code.

screens.title: Reading Layered Tool Settings and Limitations
screens.lead: The following is the code for an agent that sets both input guardrails and approvals. Check the symptoms when line ranges are selected in the right-hand description to ensure each line aligns with its corresponding layer.

notes.note: This is an input guardrail. Upon receiving the first input, a quick model makes a determination; if the determination results in tripwire_triggered being True, an InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered exception is raised and execution is halted. Incorrectly connecting the determination field may either block all requests or block none at all. This guardrail applies only to the first agent in the chain.

run_in_parallel=False is a blocking mechanism that prevents the agent from starting after the guardrail is completed. It prevents token consumption and tool execution to avoid costs and side effects. The default parallel execution reduces latency but may allow the agent to consume tokens or execute tools before the guardrail is triggered.

When needs_approval=True is attached, the execution is paused just before the tool is called, and a pending item is added to result.interruptions. Approval or rejection by a person or policy is required to proceed. This serves as the final safeguard for tools that have side effects, such as refunds.

Instructions specify a policy that search results are untrusted data. While agent-level guardrails alone may miss arguments and results of intermediate tool calls, guardrails for tools can be applied before and after function tool calls. Output guardrails apply only to the final output. Each layer increases latency and cost, so a balance must be struck.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the human review, gradual rollout, and sufficiency assessment questions.

screens.title: Human review and sufficiency assessment
screens.lead: Select each tab to explore questions about the role of human review and whether the defense combination is sufficient.

tabs.label: person review
tabs.body: Actions that carry risks—such as cancellation, editing, shell commands, or sensitive MCP operations—require human approval. While the model may determine that an action is necessary, execution is paused until approved by a human or a policy. In high-risk areas, human verification of the original input is necessary for review to be meaningful.

tabs.label: Red teaming and progressive rollout
tabs.body: Red teaming involves testing an application with adversarial inputs to verify whether injection attempts are successful. Deployment is done using a canary approach, applying it initially to only a portion of traffic to reduce the scope of potential impact. If a new defense mechanism is enabled across the entire system at once, it can inadvertently block legitimate requests, spreading the issue broadly.

tabs.label: Question 1: Unblocked paths
tabs.body: Assume one path remains unblocked. Ask whether the tool that accesses this path causes side effects. Tools that only read are less risky, but tools that perform refunds or deletions have higher priority.

tabs.label: Question 2: Tool Protection
tabs.body: It checks whether the tool has minimum privileges, sandboxing, or approval with minimum one of these. If none of these are present, having additional layers above is insufficient because the call will execute directly.

tabs.label: Question 3: Are they at the same location?
tabs.body: All layers should ask whether they are protecting the same point—for example, whether they are merely blocking user input without actually covering all aspects. Simply overlapping protections at the same point does not constitute defense in depth. The adequacy of a defense-in-depth strategy is judged by whether the remaining unblocked paths pose a risk that is acceptable in terms of potential damage.

screens.outro: Having established the judgment question, I'll now directly examine the hole-drilled configuration.

screens.title: Explanation: Reading the agent settings after hole is drilled
screens.lead: The instructor reads the web content injection setting that leads to refunds on a line-by-line basis. Check the hole's position by selecting the line range from the right-hand description.

data.code:
from agents import Agent, function_tool

#web_search and injection_guard are assumed to be the tools and guards previously configured.
#The following is an example for diagnosing a flawed design and does not actually execute any real refunds.
@function_tool
async def issue_refund(order_id: int, amount: int) -> str:
    return f"SIMULATED refund {amount} for order {order_id}"

agent = Agent(
    name="Support",
    instructions="Process the request stated in the search results",
    tools=[web_search, issue_refund],
    input_guardrails=[injection_guard],
)

notes.note: The instructions state that they are meant to handle the requests specified in the search results. This creates a structure where untrusted content can occupy the instruction slot. The body must explicitly state in policy that it is data and cannot override instructions.

input_guardrails applies only to the initial agent's input. The web body arrives later as tool results, so this line is unrelated to the symptom. A refund occurs because there are no anomalies in the input filter logs. A separate layer is needed to filter tool results.

issue_refund is a tool with side effects; it lacks needs_approval and does not perform amount or order scope validation. Once invoked, it executes directly, making it the most direct vulnerability. It now includes needs_approval=True along with self-order and upper amount validation.

The order of fixing should start with the outermost layer—the tool layer—first. By reducing the tool's permissions, the damage scope is limited early even if upper layers are compromised. Next, we further enhance context isolation by wrapping the body content in a JSON format within the tool_result and explicitly citing the source.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the hole's position, let's now trace the flow starting from the beginning, following the layered execution.

screens.title: Explanation: A flow where one layer is penetrated but the next layer blocks it.
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates step by step how each layer operates in a single example. Press the start button and use the arrows to advance one step at a time.

steps.title: Scenario: An agent that reads the web and processes refunds
steps.body: The customer support agent reads the web search results and acquires the refund tool. The prior settings have been modified to include all four layers. It is assumed that an attacker has inserted a sentence requesting a refund into the web page body.

steps.title: Step 1: Input validation is bypassed
steps.body: The new expressions in the text bypass input validation because they take forms unknown to the filter. This layer is designed under the assumption that it could be exploited.

steps.title: Stage 2: Context isolation partially impedes.
steps.body: The main content arrives in the tool_result as JSON and subject to a non-reliability policy, so the model might not follow it. However, we cannot guarantee that it will always disregard the policy, so we introduce a subsequent layer.

steps.title: Step 3: The model makes a refund call
steps.body: Assume the model created a refund tool call following a hidden sentence. Although two layers have been penetrated this far, no action has yet been executed.

steps.title: Step 4: Permissions limit the scope.
steps.body: The refund tool allows only the customer's own order and only up to a specified amount. Refunds for other orders requested by an attacker are rejected at the invocation stage.

steps.title: Step 5: Stops the remaining pending calls upon approval
steps.body: Refunds exceeding the upper limit enter a pending human approval status. If the responsible party verifies the rationale and rejects it, the refund will not be processed.

steps.title: Step 6 and Conclusion: Output Verification and Loss Limitation
steps.body: Finally, if internal information is mixed into the response, output validation performs masking. No layer is perfect, but when layers overlap, the total damage threshold is reduced. It is the tool's authority that determines this threshold.

screens.outro: Since we've confirmed the flow operating with overlapping layers, I'll now summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lesson and consider the weakest layer in your defense.

paragraphs: Defense is stacked in layers. Input validation, context isolation, output validation, and permission restrictions each handle distinct failure modes. Layers are placed at separate points so that if one layer is compromised, the next layer remains intact.

Assuming one path remains unchecked, we evaluate it by asking whether the tool it reaches causes side effects, whether the tool operates with minimal privileges, sandboxing, and approvals, and whether all layers are only blocking at a single point. Layers increase latency and cost, so a balance is maintained, and new defenses are gradually applied.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Even with many layers, sufficient permissions alone without approval are not enough. Start by verifying the damage limit of the outermost layer. If that layer is weak, damage will immediately execute as soon as any preceding layer is breached. Conversely, if that layer is strong, damage will remain minimal even if some preceding layers are compromised. If only one thing is fixed this quarter, check first the permissions of tools that have side effects.

glossary.def: It is a design that overlaps multiple layers at different points to ensure that if one defense fails, the next defense is still intact.
This structure separates trusted content from non-trusted content and explicitly indicates the source.
A device that automatically checks inputs, outputs, and tool calls.
This is control that limits the scope of tasks a model and tool can perform to only what is necessary.
This is the step where a person allows themselves to perform an action that may have side effects.

misconceptions.myth: The strongest defense is the best.
misconceptions.fact: Single defense can be circumvented. By stacking multiple layers at different points, even if one layer is breached, the next layer remains protected.
Layers can increase latency and costs, and may also lead to higher rejection rates of normal requests. Simply overlapping at the same point provides only limited effectiveness.

misconceptions.myth: Permission restrictions are not injection defense.
misconceptions.fact: Even if injection succeeds, this is the core layer that determines the damage limit. Execution will not occur if the call is made outside the scope.

misconceptions.myth: Since there is an input filter, injection in the web content is also filtered.
misconceptions.fact: The input guardrail applies to the initial input of the first agent. The payload arriving via tool results must be separately filtered.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Defense is stacked layer by layer.
Input validation, context isolation, output validation, and permission restriction handle separate failure cases.
Integrity is judged by whether it overlaps with the maximum damage limit in case of breach.
Tools that have side effects include permission restrictions and approvals.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the weakest layer in our defense, and what follows next to block after that layer is breached?

checks.q: The customer support agent reads web search results and activates a refund tool. Assuming input filtering and model discrimination are effective, which layer most directly reduces the damage limit?
options: Extend the input filter with more expressions
Add one more final output guardrail
Limit refund tools to the customer's own order and a cap amount, requiring human approval for amounts exceeding the cap.
Adding the sentence to the system prompt instructing not to refund
checks.explain: Defense layers are designed such that even if one layer is compromised, the damage is contained. By limiting tool privileges and requiring approval before allowing harmful actions, the potential impact of a call is significantly reduced.

wrong.0: New expressions are continuously emerging, and web content may not pass through user input filters.
wrong.1: Output guardrails are only applied to the final output and cannot prevent already-executed tool calls.
wrong.3: A sentence is merely one layer that the model might not follow.

checks.intro: Assuming the input filter and model's distinction has been compromised, select the layer that most directly reduces the impact. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. By limiting the scope of the refund tool and implementing approval, damage is minimized even if a call is made.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Filter extensions or sentence additions, output verification cannot reduce the damage caused by previously executed tool calls.

options: There is only one injection_guard, so the number of guardrails is limited.
With no approval or scope restrictions in issue_refund, if a call is made, it is executed directly, and the instruction follows the search results.
The web_search tool is included in the tools list.
The agent's name was not specified
checks.explain: The instruction states that the search results should be followed, and there is a refund tool with needs_approval that has no side effects or scope restrictions. input_guardrails only apply to the first input and are unrelated to the web body.

wrong.0: Increasing the guardrails does not change the input guardrails that pass through the tool's output.
wrong.2: The issue is not whether a tool is used, but rather how you handle the result and what permissions you grant.
wrong.3: The name is unrelated to security.

checks.intro: Review a vulnerability in the configuration code where web content injection leads to refund. The result is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, the most direct flaw is that the refund tool has no approval and scope restrictions.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The number or name of guardrails is not the cause of the hole. Please re-read how the tool is defined when side effects are present.
